core: The working definition of compound interest: interest earned on both the original amount (principal) and previously earned interest — interest on interest — attributed to OpenStax's Principles of Finance and corroborated by the SEC's Investor.gov glossary

Simple versus compound interest: simple pays only on the principal each period; compound pays on the growing balance, with the original worked example $1,000 at 10% for 3 years (simple gives $300 of interest, compound gives $331, arithmetic shown)
The compounding table: year-by-year growth shown in words — year, start balance, interest earned, end balance
Compounding frequency named: annual, monthly, daily — more frequent compounding grows faster at the same stated rate, stated simply
The long game: small one-time amounts grow surprisingly large over decades, with an original example
Compound interest and debt: the same engine works against borrowers (the honest flip side), with an original credit card example
The honest framing: compound interest rewards time and punishes delay, with an original start-early-versus-late comparison
supporting: The accelerating-growth effect: because prior interest earns interest, money grows in larger increments the longer it stays invested (OpenStax Section 7.2)
Effective versus stated rates: when compounding occurs more than once a year, the true annual rate is higher than the stated rate appears to be (OpenStax Section 8.4)
The dynamics of compounding apply in either direction — saver or debtor (OpenStax Section 8.4)
CFI's components of compound interest: principal, interest rate, compounding frequency, and time horizon; the longer the time horizon, the larger the ending value (CFI Compound Interest)
outOfScope: Time value of money as a general concept (sibling topic: finance:foundations:time-value-of-money; referenced only)
Future value and present value formulas as standalone topics (sibling topics: finance:foundations:future-value, finance:foundations:present-value; referenced only)
Interest rates as a topic — how rates are set and what drives them (sibling topic: finance:foundations:interest-rates; referenced only)
Savings-depth material such as budgeting, contribution plans, and account types (owned by the personal-finance subject)
The rule of 72 and other estimation shortcuts (named as approaches only, not taught at this level)
Loan amortization schedules and bond math (sibling finance topics own these; not taught here)

claims.claim: Compound interest is interest earned on the original principal plus previously earned interest — 'interest on interest'.
Simple interest pays only on the original principal each period, while compound interest pays on the growing balance from the second period onward.
In the original worked example, $1,000 at 10% for 3 years earns $300 of total interest under simple interest and $331 under compound interest (end balances $1,300 and $1,331).
Because previously earned interest also earns interest, money grows in larger and larger increments the longer it is left invested — the compounding effect accelerates growth over time.

At the same stated annual rate, more frequent compounding (monthly or daily rather than annual) produces a larger ending balance because interest joins the balance sooner and begins earning its own interest.

When interest compounds more than once per year, the effective annual rate is higher than the stated rate appears to be; the credit-card example of 1.5% per month compounds to an effective annual rate of 19.56%, not the intuitive 18%.
The compounding mechanism applies in either direction: the same dynamics that grow a saver's balance also grow a borrower's unpaid debt.

The four components of compound interest are the principal, the interest rate, the compounding frequency, and the time horizon; the longer the time horizon, the more interest payments can be made and the larger the ending value.

conflictingEvidence: No conflicting evidence found among the consulted sources. OpenStax (Section 7.2), the SEC Investor.gov glossary, and CFI state the same working definition — interest paid on principal and on accumulated interest — with no substantive disagreement on the simple-versus-compound contrast, the effect of compounding frequency on effective annual rate, or the symmetric application to borrowers. CFI's 'essentially a risk-free way to generate gains' phrasing was treated as promotional and not used; the lesson's honest framing acknowledges that compounding is a mechanism whose direction depends on whether one is saving or borrowing.
rightsIssues: OpenStax Principles of Finance pages carry a footer barring LLM ingestion without permission; used REFERENCE_ONLY with facts restated in original prose and the working definition attributed. Investor.gov is a U.S. federal government site (public domain content). CFI used REFERENCE_ONLY; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Finance, Section 7.2: Time Value of Money (TVM) Basics
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook). Read live via HTTP from openstax.org on 2026-08-21. Supports: the working definition — compound interest is interest earned in later periods on top of interest earned in earlier periods; put simply, interest that is earned on interest; simple interest applying to year 1 while compound interest ('interest on interest') applies from year 2; the $1,000-at-4% two-year arithmetic (Year 1: 1,000 x 0.04 = 40.00; Year 2: 1,040 x 0.04 = 41.60; the additional $1.60 is interest on the first year's interest; end value $1,081.60); and the long-game acceleration — a $1,000 deposit at 4% reaching $1,480.24 at 10 years and $7,106.68 at 50 years, with money growing in larger and larger increments the longer it is left in an interest-bearing account. Page footer bars LLM ingestion; respected — facts restated in original prose, working definition attributed.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Finance, Section 8.4: Stated versus Effective Rates
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook). Read live via HTTP from openstax.org on 2026-08-21. Supports: the effective interest rate reflecting compounding within a one-year period; when compounding occurs more than once per year the true annual rate is higher than appears; the credit card example (1.5% per month on unpaid balances compounding to an effective annual rate of 19.56% rather than the intuitive 18%); the month-by-month compounded-interest table (Table 8.6); and the principle that the dynamics of the time value of money apply in either direction — to a debtor paying off an obligation or an investor hoping for more frequent compounding. sourceRecords.title: Compound Interest
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B (reputable secondary). Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Supports: compound interest as interest payments made on the sum of the original principal and the previously paid interest; 'interest on interest' as the easier way to think of it, with the payment amount based on the changing balance each period rather than fixed at the original principal; the four components — principal, interest rate, compounding frequency (typically monthly, quarterly, or annual), and time horizon; and the longer the time horizon, the more interest payments that can be made and the larger the ending account value. CFI's claim that compounding is 'essentially a risk-free way to generate gains' was not used; the lesson keeps the honest framing that the mechanism works in either direction. Facts restated in original prose; no wording reproduced.
